extracted.intended_audience: literate readers of The Spectator — general public, critics, playwrights, actors, and politically engaged citizens
extracted.subtask_description: Early-18th-century periodical essays giving prescriptive and evaluative guidance on government, liberty, theatrical taste, literary criticism, and social conduct for a cultivated public. Contains criteria for judging constitutions, plays, critics, and moral behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for established national religion and government
rubrics_metrics.description: I look upon it as a peculiar Happiness, that were I to choose of what Religion I would be, and under what Government I would live, I should most certainly give the Preference to that Form of Religion and Government which is established in my own Country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preference is defended as arising from reason and conviction but might be called an "honest Prejudice" rooted in love of country; presented as an allowable evaluative stance when judging forms of government and religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of reasonable government and liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: That Form of Government appears to me the most reasonable, which is most conformable to the Equality that we find in human Nature, provided it be consistent with publick Peace and Tranquillity. This is what may properly be called Liberty, which exempts one Man from Subjection to another so far as the Order and Oeconomy of Government will permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty should reach every individual and not be confined to particular branches; partial liberty that excludes others only aggravates injustice by comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative composition for preserving liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: This Liberty is best preserved, where the Legislative Power is lodged in several Persons, especially if those Persons are of different Ranks and Interests; ... the greatest Security a People can have for their Liberty, is when the Legislative Power is in the Hands of Persons so happily distinguished, that by providing for the particular Interests of their several Ranks, they are providing for the whole Body of the People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legislature composed of multiple, diverse estates (different ranks/interests) ties particular interests to public welfare; single or homogeneous legislatures tend toward tyranny or narrow factional interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal number of legislative bodies (mixed government)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both these great Authors give the Pre-eminence to a mixt Government, consisting of three Branches, the Regal, the Noble, and the Popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One legislative body is tyranny; two bodies lack a casting voice and will be consumed by disputes; three branches (regal, noble, popular) best reproduce a balanced mixed government (Polybius/Cicero applied to English constitution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient executive/regal authority to avoid dictatorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Had the Consuls been invested with the Regal Authority to as great a Degree as our Monarchs, there would never have been any Occasions for a Dictatorship, which had in it the Power of all the three Orders, and ended in the Subversion of the whole Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An executive that lacks appropriate regal authority can create governance gaps that invite extraordinary powers (dictatorship); institutional design must give branches adequate, distinct powers to function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of government by likelihood of tyranny and human fallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Prince is a Man of Wisdom and Virtue, it is indeed happy for his People that he is absolute; but since in the common Run of Mankind, for one that is Wise and Good you find ten of a contrary Character, it is very dangerous for a Nation to stand to its Chance, or to have its publick Happiness or Misery depend on the Virtues or Vices of a single Person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of government should be judged by their vulnerability to corrupt or vicious rulers; absolute rule is risky because power tends to corrupt and removes moral inhibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty and prosperity as conditions for learning and arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Riches and Plenty are the natural Fruits of Liberty, and where these abound, Learning and all the Liberal Arts will immediately lift up their Heads and flourish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy should be evaluated on whether it produces ease and plenty that enable leisure for speculation, reading, and the liberal arts; despotism and poverty debase minds and stifle learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism tends to ignorance and barbarity
rubrics_metrics.description: This natural Tendency of Despotic Power to Ignorance and Barbarity... is, I think, an unanswerable Argument against that Form of Government, as it shews how repugnant it is to the Good of Mankind, and the Perfection of human Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical/historical evidence (e.g., Augustus, Eastern nations) to judge political systems: prevalence of slavery/despotism correlates with lack of learning and cultural degeneracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representing high rank on stage by greatness of sentiment, not props
rubrics_metrics.description: the Persons are of the highest Quality in Life, even that of Princes; but their Quality is not represented by the Poet with Direction that Guards and Waiters should follow them in every Scene, but their Grandeur appears in Greatness of Sentiment[s], flowing from Minds worthy their Condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights should show noble characters' rank through elevated thoughts and maxims, not merely through stage-trappings or supernumerary guards; true grandeur is moral/intellectual, not decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character greatness founded on superior thoughts and maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a Character truly Great, this Author understands that it should have its Foundation in superior Thoughts and Maxims of Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or judging characters (esp. heroic figures), prioritize internal moral/philosophical stature and consistent maxims over external circumstance or dramatic contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of passion within rules of decency and good-breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: The Town has an Opportunity of doing itself Justice in supporting the Representation of Passion, Sorrow, Indignation, even Despair itself, within the Rules of Decency, Honour and Good-breeding;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic performances should evoke strong emotions but remain decorous and honourable—passion should not descend into indecency or vulgarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft: keep scenes busy and parts freshly dressed for taste
rubrics_metrics.description: To supply this, he recommended to the Players to be very careful in their Scenes, and above all Things, that every Part should be perfectly new dressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers/actors should attend to contemporary taste: lively scenes and refreshed costumes/parts attract audiences; staging choices can influence reception even if the work is 'nature' in content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for visitors courting young women to declare intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: all Visitants who frequent Families wherein there are young Females, are forthwith required to declare themselves, or absent from Places where their Presence banishes such as would pass their Time more to the Advantage of those whom they visit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social conduct guidance: suitors should be explicit about their intentions; families should expect transparency to protect young women from ambiguous or harmful courtship (practical enforcement implied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical writing: death-accounts as universally affecting and instructive
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing in History which is so improving to the Reader, as those Accounts which we meet with of the Deaths of eminent Persons, and of their Behaviour in that dreadful Season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians and biographers should include manner of death and last behaviour as instructive, universally affecting material that teaches moral lessons and engages readers more than battles or triumphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary learning and logical clearness for a critic
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient, that a Man who sets up for a Judge in Criticism, should have perused the Authors above mentioned, unless he has also a clear and Logical Head. Without this Talent he is perpetually puzzled and perplexed amidst his own Blunders...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic needs broad learning (classical authors, ancients and moderns) and strong reasoning/logic; mere reading is insufficient—ability to order thoughts and convey them clearly is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish words from things; orderly thinking (Locke)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Locke's Essay on Human Understanding would be thought a very odd Book for a Man to make himself Master of, who would get a Reputation by Critical Writings; though at the same time it is very certain, that an Author who has not learned the Art of distinguishing between Words and Things, and of ranging his Thoughts, and setting them in proper Lights, whatever Notions he may have, will lose himself in Confusion and Obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics/authors should heed philosophical principles (Locke) to avoid mistaking linguistic forms for ideas and must organize thoughts coherently to communicate criticism effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic should praise excellencies and seek concealed beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: A true Critick ought to dwell rather upon Excellencies than Imperfections, to discover the concealed Beauties of a Writer, and communicate to the World such things as are worth their Observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism emphasizes strengths and uncovers overlooked virtues; focusing only on small faults is an easy and common vice of inferior critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ridicule and improper wit in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a Mirth as this is always unseasonable in a Critick, as it rather prejudices the Reader than convinces him, and is capable of making a Beauty, as well as a Blemish, the Subject of Derision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be serious and instructive; using wit or ridicule to show off cleverness is unfair and can mislead readers and unjustly tarnish passages of genuine merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value genius above pedantic exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Productions of a great Genius, with many Lapses and Inadvertencies, are infinitely preferable to the Works of an inferior kind of Author, which are scrupulously exact and conformable to all the Rules of correct Writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating literature, prefer overall force and original genius over mechanical perfection that lacks greatness of thought; tolerate lapses in otherwise great works.
